The chief concern is a several-year history of slowly progressive purple spots on both feet that increased in number and size. Clinically, these are multiple purple papules and plaques on the dorsum of the feet and around the ankles, some crusted. In an older man, bilateral violaceous acral lesions raise concern for a vascular proliferation, especially Kaposi sarcoma, but the diagnosis must be reconciled with the biopsy.

Salient positive findings include: chronic, gradual enlargement over years; bilateral acral distribution on feet/ankles; violaceous papules and plaques; and histology showing a vascular lesion extending from papillary to reticular dermis in a lobular pattern, composed mainly of dilated blood-filled thin-walled spaces with some thick-walled vessels, hemosiderin deposition, chronic inflammation, and focal immature vascular clefts with extravasated erythrocytes and mild endothelial atypia. These features indicate a benign-to-borderline vascular proliferation with hemorrhagic change. The absence of systemic symptoms, lymphadenopathy, visceral involvement, and negative HIV serology are important clinical context points.

Pertinent negatives are especially helpful. There is no spindle cell proliferation on histology, which argues strongly against Kaposi sarcoma despite the clinical resemblance. There is no mention of dissecting irregular anastomosing vascular channels infiltrating collagen, marked atypia, or multilayered endothelium to support angiosarcoma. The lesion is not described as a simple targetoid solitary papule typical of hobnail hemangioma, and histology instead shows larger dilated vessels with hemosiderin and focal papillary-dermal slitlike immature areas. There is also no systemic disease or immunosuppression to support epidemic or iatrogenic Kaposi sarcoma.

The leading differential is acroangiodermatitis (pseudo-Kaposi sarcoma), particularly the Mali type or a related acral reactive vascular proliferation. It fits the bilateral lesions on the feet/ankles of an older man and the histology of capillary/venous proliferation with thick- and thin-walled vessels, hemosiderin, extravasated erythrocytes, and inflammation. Acroangiodermatitis can clinically mimic Kaposi sarcoma and may show vascular clefts and mild endothelial atypia, but lacks the spindle-cell fascicles characteristic of Kaposi sarcoma.

Kaposi sarcoma is the main competing diagnosis because of the violaceous plaques on the feet and the focal slitlike vascular spaces with extravasated erythrocytes. However, it is less likely because HIV serology is negative, there is no systemic involvement, and most importantly the biopsy lacks spindle cell proliferation, which is a key histologic feature of Kaposi sarcoma.

Another consideration is verrucous hemangioma or other benign venous/lymphatic vascular malformation, given the hyperkeratotic epidermis and dilated vascular spaces. However, the age of onset in late adulthood, bilateral multifocal acral distribution, and pseudo-Kaposi-like clinical appearance make this less fitting. Angiosarcoma is low likelihood because the course is indolent over years and histology shows only mild atypia without destructive infiltrative malignant features.

Narrowing to a single diagnosis: the combination of bilateral slowly progressive violaceous acral plaques, absence of systemic disease, and biopsy showing lobular dilated vascular proliferation with hemosiderin and extravasated erythrocytes but no spindle cell proliferation most strongly supports acroangiodermatitis (pseudo-Kaposi sarcoma).
Differential diagnoses:
- Acroangiodermatitis (pseudo-Kaposi sarcoma) (high): Older man with bilateral slowly progressive violaceous papules/plaques on feet and ankles; histology shows lobular dermal vascular proliferation with thin- and thick-walled vessels, hemosiderin, extravasated erythrocytes, chronic inflammation, and crucially no spindle cell proliferation.
- Kaposi sarcoma (medium): Clinical appearance of purple acral plaques and focal slitlike immature vascular clefts with extravasated erythrocytes can mimic KS, but HIV is negative, there is no systemic involvement, and biopsy lacks spindle cell proliferation.
- Angiosarcoma (low): Vascular lesion with mild endothelial atypia is noted, but the lesions are indolent over several years and histology does not show the marked atypia or infiltrative malignant vascular channels expected.
Final diagnosis: Acroangiodermatitis (pseudo-Kaposi sarcoma)
